title: Japan Beyond Tokyo and Kyoto: Where to Go When the Classics Are Full
metaDescription: Kanazawa, Takayama, the Kiso Valley, Tohoku, Shikoku and Kyushu — where to go in Japan when Kyoto is overwhelmed, with routes and rail advice.
excerpt: Kyoto now receives more visitors than it can comfortably hold. The rest of Japan is extraordinary and comparatively empty.
author: Travel Editors
content:
Japan's visitor numbers have grown faster than almost anywhere, and the growth has concentrated on a single corridor: Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, with a stop at Mount Fuji. Kyoto in particular now has days when its most famous streets are difficult to walk, and the city has introduced restrictions in parts of Gion in response to visitor behaviour.

Meanwhile, most of Japan is quiet. The rail network is superb, the food is excellent everywhere, and prefectures an hour off the main line receive a fraction of the visitors.

Here is where to go instead — or, better, in addition.

## Kanazawa

The most direct substitute for Kyoto, and the strongest recommendation on this list.

Kanazawa escaped bombing in the war, which means its historic districts are genuinely old rather than reconstructed. It has:

- **Kenroku-en**, one of Japan's three great gardens, at its best in snow
- **A preserved samurai district** (Nagamachi) with earthen walls and residences
- **Three geisha districts**, including Higashi Chaya, with teahouses you can enter
- **The 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art**, genuinely excellent
- **Omicho Market**, and some of the best seafood in Japan
- **Gold leaf craft** — the city produces almost all of Japan's

Two and a half hours from Tokyo by shinkansen. Two days is right.

![Japan travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1624253321171-1be53e12f5f4?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Takayama and the Japanese Alps

**Takayama** sits in a mountain basin with a beautifully preserved Edo-period merchant quarter, morning markets, and sake breweries you can visit.

Nearby:

- **Shirakawa-go** — steep thatched farmhouses in a valley, UNESCO-listed, spectacular under snow. A day trip, and busy at peak times
- **Kamikochi** — an alpine valley open roughly April to November, with one of Japan's finest easy walks along the Azusa River
- **Hida-Furukawa** — a smaller, quieter Takayama, twenty minutes away

## The Kiso Valley and the Nakasendo

The old post road between Kyoto and Edo, with several preserved post towns along it. The **Magome-to-Tsumago** walk is around eight kilometres over a pass, well marked, and one of the most satisfying half-days in Japan. Both towns have inns where you can stay in a traditional building with a kaiseki dinner.

Arrive in the late afternoon, stay overnight, and you get the towns after the day-trippers leave.

## Tohoku: The North

The most under-visited region of Honshu, and the one that rewards a longer trip.

- **Matsushima** — a bay scattered with pine-covered islands, traditionally one of Japan's three great views
- **Yamadera** — a temple complex climbing a thousand steps up a wooded mountainside
- **Ginzan Onsen** — a gas-lit hot spring street of wooden inns, extraordinary in winter snow
- **Nyuto Onsen** — remote, rustic hot springs including milky-white outdoor baths
- **Hirosaki** — a castle with arguably Japan's best cherry blossom, weeks later than Tokyo's, which means you can catch the season after it has ended further south
- **Aomori's Nebuta Festival** in August — enormous illuminated floats

Tohoku is where to go if you want traditional rural Japan without competition.

![Japan travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1503899036084-c55cdd92da26?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Shikoku

The smallest of the main islands and the least visited.

- **The 88 Temple Pilgrimage** — a 1,200-kilometre circuit that can be walked in sections rather than in full
- **The Iya Valley** — deep gorges, vine bridges, and genuine remoteness
- **Naoshima and Teshima** — the art islands in the Inland Sea, with museums by Tadao Ando and installations in abandoned houses. Genuinely unlike anywhere else
- **Matsuyama** — Dogo Onsen, one of Japan's oldest bathhouses
- **Kotohira** — a shrine at the top of 785 steps

## Kyushu

The southern island, with volcanoes, the country's best hot springs and a distinct food culture.

- **Beppu and Yufuin** — the onsen capitals, with an extraordinary density of hot springs
- **Kurokawa Onsen** — a small, beautifully preserved hot spring town where a single pass lets you bathe at multiple inns
- **Mount Aso** — one of the world's largest caldera
- **Nagasaki** — layered history, a dramatic harbour setting, and a genuinely moving peace memorial
- **Yakushima** — an island of ancient cedar forest and extremely heavy rainfall, the landscape that inspired Princess Mononoke
- **Fukuoka** — outstanding food, particularly tonkotsu ramen and the yatai street food stalls

## Hokkaido

The northern island, and the reason Japanese travellers head north in summer.

- **Summer** — lavender fields in Furano, hiking in Daisetsuzan, cool temperatures while the rest of Japan swelters
- **Winter** — the best powder snow in the world, at Niseko and Furano
- **Food** — seafood, dairy, ramen, and a growing wine industry
- **Shiretoko** — a UNESCO wilderness peninsula with brown bears

## How to Actually Plan This

**Use the rail network properly.** The Japan Rail Pass is only worth it if you are covering long distances frequently — do the arithmetic against individual tickets rather than assuming. Regional passes, which cover a single area for less, are often the better buy for the itineraries above.

**Stay in ryokan and minshuku** outside the cities. A traditional inn with dinner and breakfast included is frequently better value than a city hotel, and it is the experience itself.

**Book accommodation early** in the small towns. Ginzan Onsen, Kurokawa and the Kiso Valley post towns have very limited inventory and sell out months ahead in peak seasons.

**Combine, do not replace.** Tokyo is genuinely worth several days. The argument is not to avoid the famous places but to avoid spending your whole trip in the corridor between them.

**Avoid the peak weeks** if you possibly can: cherry blossom in late March and early April, Golden Week at the start of May, Obon in mid-August, and peak autumn colour in November. Late May, June, early July, and early December are quiet, pleasant and dramatically cheaper.

## A Two-Week Alternative Route

- **Days 1–3** — Tokyo
- **Day 4** — Takayama
- **Day 5** — Shirakawa-go, then Kanazawa
- **Days 6–7** — Kanazawa
- **Days 8–9** — Kiso Valley, walking the Nakasendo and staying in a post town
- **Days 10–11** — Kyoto, briefly and early in the mornings
- **Days 12–14** — Naoshima and the Inland Sea, or fly to Kyushu for onsen

That route sees more of Japan than the standard itinerary, costs less, and involves considerably less queueing.

Japan rewards booking the fixed points early and leaving the rest loose — the ryokan and the rail legs are what constrain everything else. Getting those into a shared plan first, then filling the days around them, is the sequence that works; **Trypinn** makes the constraint visible so you are not discovering it after the flights are bought.
